## Two Hands Make One Visible Wrench {#sec-lay-ch12}

## A Concrete Picture

Turn a steering wheel by pushing down with one hand and pulling up with the
other. The two forces can nearly cancel as a net force on the wheel's center,
yet together they create a clear turning effect. Now squeeze the wheel equally
from both sides. The internal load in your hands rises while the wheel's motion
may not change at all.

Two hands on a golf grip create the same distinction. The club responds to the
combined **wrench**: net force plus net moment about a chosen point. The arms and
wrists may experience very different individual forces while producing the same
club wrench. Club motion alone cannot reveal the hidden allocation.

![Equal and Opposite Hand Forces Produce a Turning Couple Whose Magnitude Grows With Grip Separation.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_two_hand_couple.svg){#fig-lay-two-hand-couple width=96% fig-alt="Two grip diagrams show equal and opposite hand forces at narrow and wide separations, with the wider separation producing a larger turning couple despite zero resultant force."}

## How the Mechanism Works

Let hand forces be $\mathbf F_L$ and $\mathbf F_R$ at positions
$\mathbf r_L$ and $\mathbf r_R$ relative to club reference $O$. Include direct
hand or wrist moments $\mathbf M_L$ and $\mathbf M_R$. The equivalent club wrench
is

$$
\mathbf F_O=\mathbf F_L+\mathbf F_R,
$$

$$
\mathbf M_O=\mathbf M_L+\mathbf M_R+
\mathbf r_L\times\mathbf F_L+
\mathbf r_R\times\mathbf F_R.
$$

All components use the same orthonormal axes at the same instant; each position
vector points from $O$ to its contact. The moments are contact moments exerted
on the club, not automatically anatomical wrist joint torques. For a rigid club
with known inertia and all other loads specified, the combined wrench determines
the hands' contribution to acceleration. Many allocations produce the same sum.
A flexible club also has deformation modes that a single resultant does not describe.

### Common and Differential Modes

Define $\mathbf F_c=(\mathbf F_L+\mathbf F_R)/2$ and
$\mathbf F_d=(\mathbf F_L-\mathbf F_R)/2$. Let $\mathbf r_c$ locate the contact midpoint
relative to $O$, and $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_L-\mathbf r_R$ point from the right
contact to the left. Then, exactly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F_O&=2\mathbf F_c,\\
\mathbf M_O&=\mathbf M_L+\mathbf M_R
 +2\mathbf r_c\times\mathbf F_c+\mathbf d\times\mathbf F_d.
\end{aligned}
$$

About the midpoint, the common force has no moment. About another point it
usually does. Only the part of $\mathbf F_d$ perpendicular to $\mathbf d$
creates the differential force couple. Its axial part changes internal loading
without changing the wrench.

If we add $+\boldsymbol\eta$ to one hand and
$-\boldsymbol\eta$ to the other, resultant force stays unchanged. Depending on
contact geometry, moment may change or remain unchanged along certain null-space
directions. This is the mathematical source of hidden internal loading.

### What Inverse Dynamics Can Identify

If full club motion and inertia are known well enough, inverse dynamics can
estimate the required net external wrench. Isolating the hands requires
subtracting gravity, aerodynamic loads and any ball-contact load using the same
boundary and reference point. Impact may require an impulse balance rather than
a smoothly differentiated acceleration. Clubhead position alone does not supply
the complete rigid-body state or flexible-shaft motion. Even a perfectly known
hand resultant cannot identify its split without additional measurements or assumptions.

A minimum-norm allocation is a reproducible mathematical choice. It is not a
measurement of how a golfer used the arms. A muscle-effort optimization is still
model-dependent. Instrumented grips with force and moment sensing provide the
most direct route to individual hand wrenches.

### The Invisible Axial Push--Pull Mode

For two point forces at distinct locations, with no free contact moments, the map is

$$
G=\begin{bmatrix}I&I\\\left[\mathbf r_L\right]_\times&\left[\mathbf r_R\right]_\times\end{bmatrix},
\qquad [\mathbf r]_\times\mathbf f=\mathbf r\times\mathbf f.
$$

Zero resultant force requires opposite force increments. Zero moment then requires
$\mathbf d\times\boldsymbol\eta=0$: the increment lies along the contact line.
The null space has dimension one, so the map has rank five. Equivalently, the
moment about the midpoint cannot have a component along $\mathbf d$ in this
point-force model. If the locations coincide, the rank drops to three and every
opposite force pair is invisible.

For distinct known contacts, an added scalar measurement sensitive to the axial
null direction closes the structural rank gap. A redundant measurement does not.
Short separation also amplifies force errors associated with transverse moment
noise, so full rank does not ensure reliable estimation. One scalar is insufficient if
each hand can also apply its own three-dimensional contact moment: the full
12-to-6 bilateral-wrench map retains a six-dimensional invisible family. The
calculation is a sensor-design result, not an anatomical result. It does not
identify wrist action, scapular action, muscle recruitment, or intentionality,
and calibrated noise, cross-talk, and moving contact centers still require
separate qualification.

These dimensions concern unconstrained linear maps. Friction, unilateral contact,
finite grip strength and allowable moments restrict physically possible loads.
Their intersection with an algebraic solution family need not have the same
dimension or contain any solution.

### Internal Force Can Matter Without Moving the Club

Hidden loading may change grip stability, friction margin, joint compression,
muscle activation and effective stiffness. The axial point-force null mode is
not itself a measurement of normal grip pressure. At a fixed state, a zero-wrench
load increment does zero power against a rigid velocity field, exactly. Its
metabolic cost and tissue loading can still be nonzero. With deformation or slip,
equal resultants can also conceal different mechanical power. There is no single
internal metric called “effort” that settles these trades. Reducing an axial null
load does not algebraically require increasing a contact moment.

This is why the technical article refuses to infer scapular recruitment from a
club couple. A proximal generalized-torque subspace can be labeled and tested in
the model, but the mapping to muscles, scapular motion, and hand pressure is not
unique.

### Action-Reaction Must Close

At a common physical interface, each force has an equal and opposite reaction.
Transform moments to the same point and axes before summing both sides. An ideal
rigid grasp uses closure constraints; a compliant grasp needs a constitutive
law with stored-energy and dissipation terms. Opposite forces do not make
contact-pair power vanish when the two sides have different velocities.

For loads on one rigid club,

$$
P_{\mathrm{hands}}=\sum_i
 (\mathbf F_i\cdot\mathbf v_i+\mathbf M_i\cdot\boldsymbol\omega)
 =\mathbf F_O\cdot\mathbf v_O+\mathbf M_O\cdot\boldsymbol\omega.
$$

Here $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf v_O+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r_i$ is the club's
velocity field in one inertial observer. Changing the reference point transports
both wrench and velocity; changing observer is a different operation. For a
deforming grip or shaft, use actual local velocities and rotations. A single
rigid-body power formula is insufficient. Power and energy residuals test these
ledgers separately from action-reaction closure.

The [archived spatial contact test](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/spatial_forward_contact_study.json)
uses MuJoCo and Pinocchio for independent kinematics and forward dynamics, but
shares the contact law and time-stepping scheme. Agreement tests those engine
implementations under shared assumptions; it cannot independently validate the
shared law. The hands are finite-mass translational carriages, not anatomical arms.

### Why Two Hands Can Create Negative Coupling

Near the late downswing, separated hand forces can produce a couple with a
negative projection onto a declared swing-plane normal. The forces need not
themselves point along that normal. Couple power is the full dot product with
angular velocity: one negative component alone does not establish negative power.
Even negative moment power can coexist with increasing club kinetic energy when
force power and other external powers outweigh it. Inertial coordinate terms are
not an extra energy source. The model asks where the couple comes from and
whether the mechanism persists in a specified forward intervention.

At fixed bounded forces, collapsing hand separation eliminates the differential
force couple; reversing $\mathbf d$ with $\mathbf F_d$ fixed reverses its sign.
Free contact moments do not vanish in either control. These geometric checks are
not predictions for a newly integrated swing: moving contacts can change forces,
constraints, commands and motion. Keeping a nonzero force couple as separation
tends to zero would require unbounded perpendicular differential force.

**Model Result:** Wrench reconstruction reveals nonunique internal modes. In the
pinned reduced spatial test, switching off the declared driver at 0.18 s retains
a negative swing-normal force couple for 0.0375 s, with minimum about
$-0.4093$ N m in both engines. This is a model-time interval, not a measured phase
of a golfer's downswing. Coincident and reversed geometry checks transport the
same achieved forces; they are algebraic controls, distinct from the integrated
driver-switch experiment. Stored energy and initial motion remain after the switch.

**Human Evidence:** Instrumented grips add information that club motion lacks,
but sensor signals and inferred hand loads must be distinguished. Koike's example
used one professional instructor and statically calibrated strain gauges, with
fixed hand reference points and neglected handle-piece inertia [@koike2016instrumented].
Choi and Park studied nine right-handed male professional golfers using a
six-axis sensor between two grip segments and inverse dynamics. Their heavier
grip, possible hand-to-hand load bypass and foam-ball impacts limit interpretation
[@koike2020]. Neither study identifies muscle recruitment or validates the present
synthetic model's hand allocation.

**Hypothesis:** Opposed arm-chain actions can generate a useful club couple while
wrists supply resistance or impedance, but only synchronized bilateral wrench
and biological measurements can test that allocation.

**Practical Interpretation:** The club can feel one net push and twist while the
two hands experience a much richer internal negotiation.

### From Two Contacts to One Club Load

Each hand can apply three force components and three moment components at its
contact reference frame. Transform both six-dimensional wrenches to one club
frame, including the moment created by each position offset, then add them. The
resultant hand wrench contributes to rigid-body acceleration together with all
other external loads and inertia. Shaft forces are internal to a whole-club
boundary; they become boundary loads when a shaft or clubhead subsystem is cut
out. Count them once at the chosen boundary. This sum is estimable in principle,
but its split between hands is not determined by club motion alone.

In a planar simplification, the arithmetic is easier: two two-dimensional forces
at separated points create a net force and an out-of-plane moment. Even there,
multiple pairs yield the same resultant. Adding equal and opposite force to the
two hands changes internal loading while leaving net force unchanged; depending
on direction, it can change the couple. Distinct point-force contacts have one
axial null direction in either two or three dimensions. Allowing full contact
wrenches increases the nullity from three in the planar model to six in space.

### Interpreting Push--Pull

The exact midpoint decomposition separates resultant force from the differential
force couple and free contact moments. This coordinate change does not claim the
nervous system controls those modes explicitly. It is a clean way to see which
parts of bilateral loading are visible at the club and which can cancel.

The distinction also clarifies “push--pull.” Equal opposition is not required.
One hand may supply a larger force, both may point partly in the same direction,
and contact moments may matter. A measured push in grip-local coordinates can
coexist with a laboratory-frame component that looks like a pull. The complete
wrench should replace verbal labels wherever data permit.

### How a Negative Couple Can Emerge

Near impact, proximal motion, club inertia, grip constraints, and contact
geometry determine the reactions required at the hands. A differential force
component acting through hand separation may project onto the swing-plane
normal with negative sign even when neither hand is commanded with an explicit
negative club torque. Calling a reaction “passive” requires a declared partition:
the same contact force can depend on active proximal commands, stored elastic
energy and inertia. State dependence alone does not establish muscular passivity.

That statement is narrower than “the scapulae passively torque the club.” The
generalized drivers can stand for many body actions. Reconstructing a negative
contact couple does not uniquely map it to shoulder-girdle motion, wrist action,
or muscle activation. The model supplies an observable prediction for bilateral
wrenches; anatomy remains a separate inference problem.

### A Worked Wrench Example

Let the hands be separated by 0.20 metres. Suppose they apply opposite 50-newton
forces perpendicular to that separation. Net force is zero and couple magnitude
is 10 newton-metres. Add the same 100-newton vector to each hand: net force becomes
200 newtons and moment about the contact midpoint remains 10 newton-metres when
free contact moments are zero. About an offset reference, include the additional
moment of the common force. If
separation drops to 0.10 metres, the same opposing forces make 5 newton-metres.

Real force vectors are not perfectly perpendicular, contact points are
distributed, and hand moments may contribute. The arithmetic nonetheless gives
testable dependencies: couple scales with perpendicular separation and force;
reversing either reverses sign; collapsing either collapses the couple. A model
or measurement pipeline should pass those controls exactly within tolerance.

### Matching the Club Task, Varying the Allocation

To compare arm-dominant and wrist-dominant strategies fairly, first specify a
club-level task: perhaps the same net wrench history or a set of terminal club
states. Solve for distinct internal allocations that meet it. Then compare
joint demands, individual hand power, co-contraction proxy, transmission state,
peak load, and sensitivity. The matched task prevents one strategy from “winning”
merely because it was asked to produce a larger club moment.

Next relax the task and optimize performance under common constraints. This
second experiment asks whether internal freedom can improve speed or robustness.
Keeping matched-task and optimized comparisons separate avoids confusing
mechanical equivalence with performance preference.

### What Bilateral Sensors Add

Separate six-axis grip sensors directly constrain each contact wrench. Pressure
mapping can reveal distributed contact and shifts in effective application point.
Shaft strain helps close the club load balance. Synchronized motion supplies
velocities for contact power and transforms sensor axes to club and laboratory
frames. Force plates and body motion support whole-system closure.

Calibration needs known loads, crosstalk characterization, thermal drift checks,
and frame registration. Grip modification can itself change behavior, so the
instrumented club should be compared with a standard club. Uncertainty in hand
position and sensor orientation should propagate to couple sign and magnitude.

### Why Closure Is Not Calibration

A [pinned synthetic sensor qualification](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/bilateral_wrench_sensor_qualification.json)
makes the distinction quantitative. Its net-wrench-only inverse closes the
resultant to numerical tolerance while giving 11.86 N component-wise RMSE across
the six hand-force components and 29.05 N RMSE for its declared axial scalar.
These are errors against synthetic ground truth. Closure tests consistency with
the supplied resultant; it does not establish that either the resultant or
allocation is physically correct.

The same controlled study separates practical measurement errors. Correcting a
declared cross-talk matrix reduces allocation RMSE from 0.94 N to 0.15 N; a 10%
error in the cross-talk correction amplitude raises it to 0.18 N; this is not
ten-percent device accuracy. Holding contact centers fixed
with the migration amplitude parameter set to 8 mm causes 2.02 N RMSE; this
parameter scales prescribed sinusoidal coordinates, not total travel. Tracking those centers
removes that modeled bias in the idealized migration case. The combined case,
with noise, residual cross-talk error and untracked migration amplitude set to 4 mm, gives
1.02 N component-wise RMSE and 3.87 N at the 95th percentile of the
six-component error-vector norm over 32 seeded trials with 301 samples each.
The percentile and RMSE use different aggregations; they are not two statistics
of one scalar hand-force error. The 8-mm and 4-mm settings are different cases.

These values come from a synthetic point-force sensor qualification, not a
physical transducer, distributed-pressure experiment, or participant study.
They define pre-acquisition acceptance tests: verify the augmented rank, report
allocation error in addition to wrench closure, calibrate cross-talk, track
effective contact centers, propagate residual calibration uncertainty, and
fail closed when any required channel or registration is absent. Governed
bilateral six-axis human data are still required to test the proposed hand,
wrist, arm, or scapular mechanisms.

### Internal Force Is Not Wasted Force

An equal-and-opposite hand mode may cancel at the club's center-of-mass force
balance while increasing grip compression, joint load, or stiffness. It may
help stabilize the clubface or may be needless co-contraction. Net club motion
cannot decide. Outcomes and internal-load measurements are required.

This is where the question of “slack” becomes scientific. If continuous
bilateral loading reduces a measurable force-development delay or perturbation
response time without excessive internal cost, preload has operational value.
If the same club task occurs with no gap or robustness difference, the proposed
benefit is unsupported. A feeling of connection is not yet a measured state.

### One Point per Hand Is Itself a Modeling Choice

Treating each hand as a single contact point is convenient, and the natural
worry is that the convenience is doing the work. A
[registered reduced-model comparison](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/articulated_distributed_grip_atlas.json)
examines one part of that question.

Each hand was replaced by one, three, or five tension fibers spread across a
30 mm band, while **total per-hand** stiffness and damping were held fixed at
1800 N/m and 18 N$\cdot$s/m, divided equally among that hand's stations. That control matters: adding contact points without
holding the total constant would silently stiffen the grip, and any change could
then be blamed on stiffness rather than on distribution.

The archived design contains 288 trajectories: twelve initial states, three
station counts, two velocity branches, two integration steps and two engines.
The 4, 10, 25 and 50 ms outputs are nested observation horizons within each
50 ms trajectory, not integration timesteps or separate trials. The steps are
1 and 0.5 ms. Initial motion supplies the starting condition; this experiment
does not use active joint drivers.

Peak single-station force reached 4.03 N. The maximum concentration of 0.77 is
the largest station-force norm divided by the sum of all station-force norms
at an instant. It is neither pressure nor a named finger's share. The summary
also reports zero transitions of whether **any station is active**. That counter
does not track every station's engagement. Indeed, the maximum fraction of
samples with fewer than all stations active is 1.0. Zero recorded global
on/off transitions therefore cannot establish that every contact stayed closed.

The maximum three-to-five-station comparison at the fine step is 0.00355. Its
implementation compares final coordinate arrays using maximum absolute component
difference divided by the larger of one and the two maximum coordinate
magnitudes. This is a registered coordinate-dependent diagnostic, not a unit-
invariant physical error or proof of convergence of forces, energy and contact
events. The stored coordinates mix translations and rotations; units and
parameterization affect the comparison. The worst normalized work-energy residual
also falls from 0.03119 to 0.01560 on timestep refinement. Passing these particular
checks supports a bounded comparison, not universal discretization convergence.

Holding total stiffness and damping fixed makes the comparison interpretable.
It does not measure grip pressure, identify finger anatomy, or model friction
or soft tissue. A number of stations is not a set of fingers. These statements
describe the pinned archive, not a new solver run or current-human validation.

### Minimum Evidence for a Human Claim

The model prediction should specify phase, frame, couple sign, magnitude range,
geometry dependence, and competing explanations. A human test should measure
bilateral wrench, motion, shaft response, and relevant activation, with
participant-held-out analysis. Only then can researchers ask whether a modeled
contact mechanism is commonly used, individually variable, or absent. Until
then, it remains a falsifiable mechanical hypothesis—not a prescription.

### Reader Lab: Explore the Hidden Mode

Start with one pair of hand forces that produces a target club wrench. Add a
small vector to one hand and subtract it from the other. Recompute the resultant.
Depending on the vector and hand separation, net force stays fixed while moment
changes. Add compensating contact moments so the full target wrench is restored.
You have constructed a distinct internal allocation with identical rigid club
loading.

Repeat while minimizing different costs: total force squared, peak wrist moment,
lead-hand load, or deviation from a measured pressure pattern. Each criterion
selects a different solution. This makes the role of regularization visible.
Without bilateral measurement, none should be called the observed allocation.

Now add simulated sensor noise and contact-position uncertainty. Estimate the
confidence interval on swing-normal couple and on each hand's contribution. A
negative mean with an interval spanning zero is not firm evidence of sign. The
lab links elementary wrench geometry to realistic qualification.

### How This Guides Product Design

The software should display net wrench and the family of compatible allocations
when individual forces are unavailable. When bilateral data exist, it should
show measured allocation with uncertainty and closure residual. Any optimized
allocation should be labeled as a model solution with its cost function.

This prevents the interface from converting hidden assumptions into anatomical
facts. It also makes the tool useful for experiment design: users can see which
sensor or manipulation would shrink the ambiguity most.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The steering wheel is rigid, symmetric, and fixed to one axis. A golf grip moves
in space, the shaft bends, wrist axes rotate, pressure is distributed, and both
arms attach to a moving body. Two point contacts are a reduction.

The common/differential transformation also does not identify comfort or intent.
The same internal wrench can arise from different muscles and co-contraction.
Technique claims need participant-level evidence.
